Animation Lab

300 fishermen dance on the festival pier, each with a 70-bone skeleton. Most are behind the camera or tiny. Choose who animates, how often, with how many bones, and where the skinning runs.

Festival pier, mid-range phone, 30 fps. Goal: animation at most 3 ms of main thread in the worst frame, and GPU at most 28 ms (the pier draws in 24.0 ms).

Lesson 039: animation cost

    What this shows

    Don't animate what nobody sees

    180 of 300 dancers are behind the camera. With the default culling mode they still evaluate 70 bones and skin 7,000 vertices every frame.

    Update rate by size on screen

    A 20-pixel dancer updated at 7.5 Hz looks the same as at 30 Hz. But update everyone on the same frame and the average hides a spike every fourth frame.

    Fewer bones, other processor

    Far dancers need 20 bones, not 70. GPU skinning moves the vertex work off the main thread, where it is cheaper, and costs GPU time instead.

    This lab is a simulation, not a measurement. It uses Lesson 039's numbers: evaluating a 70-bone skeleton 14 µs (20 bones: 4 µs); skinning 7,000 vertices at 3 ns each on the CPU, 21 µs (1,500 vertices: 4.5 µs); an off-screen dancer with Cull Update Transforms 2 µs; the animation system's fixed cost 0.5 ms; GPU skinning 1.5 ns a vertex for every visible dancer, every frame.
